records.found: On 2026-11-06 the United States trial registry first posted VITAL-H (NCT07923630), a placebo-controlled trial at the University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio, paid for by the federal health research agency ARPA-H, which plans to give two approved drugs (dapagliflozin and semaglutide tablets) or placebo to 1,200 healthy people aged 60 to 75 for 36 months, starting in January 2027 and finishing its main measurement in December 2030. This points towards the early end of the estimate, because the estimate assumes a trial of this kind starts by 2029 and here one is registered to start in 2027; but its main measure is a score of walking, balance and rising from a chair, not years free of disease or length of life, so a good result would not by itself meet the test as written. Against: a study in GeroScience on 2026-11-05 of 11,474 kidney transplant recipients found no difference in age at death between those prescribed rapamycin and those not (it is a study of records, not a controlled trial).

findings.what: Registry entry NCT07923630 first posted: 'Validation & Intervention Testing for Aging, Longevity and Healthspan (VITAL-H)', University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio with the Department of Health and Human Services (grant number marked ARPA-H). Not yet recruiting; 1,200 people aged 60 to 75 without diabetes; three groups (semaglutide tablets, dapagliflozin, placebo); 36 months of treatment plus 6 months of follow-up; estimated start 2027-01, main measurement complete 2030-12, study complete 2031-02. Main measure: the Short Physical Performance Battery score.

The university's own announcement of the same trial gave different figures: 726 adults in their 60s, three drugs (rapamycin, dapagliflozin, semaglutide) against placebo in four groups, up to 38 million dollars from ARPA-H over five years, enrolment to start in 2027. The registry entry of 2026-11-06 lists no rapamycin group and 1,200 people. I found no announcement explaining the change.

Stewart and Fitzsimmons, GeroScience, 'Rapamycin and human longevity among kidney transplant recipients surviving the first year': United States transplant registry data, 4,885 recipients prescribed rapamycin and 6,589 not, followed a median of 11 years; adjusted median age at death 64.6 against 64.3 years, no meaningful difference. Peer-reviewed; a records study, not a controlled trial. Date confirmed at Crossref.

American Heart Association news release on a meeting abstract (Scientific Sessions, Chicago, 2026-11-06 to 2026-11-09): in health records of 256,492 adults with prediabetes and obesity, those on GLP-1 drugs had a 41 per cent lower risk of death from any cause than those on metformin over about three years. Observational and not peer-reviewed, as the release itself says.
Search of the trial registry for the metformin trial designed to measure time to age-related disease (TAME) by its full title still returns no entry for it.

records.found: Nothing in the week meets the test, but three registry postings bear on it. On 2026-11-06 Epirium Bio registered a placebo-controlled trial of its drug MF-300 in 225 people aged 65 and over with age-related muscle loss (NCT07921420, starting January 2027, main measurement due June 2028); it is not a mitochondrial drug, so it would not count for this entry, but it is the kind of trial in that condition the estimate waits for. On 2026-11-09 the maker of urolithin A registered a small study of two forms of its product, and the National Institute on Aging's 180-person urolithin A trial in people 55 and over (main measure insulin release, not muscle) was updated with a start date of 2026-11-12. Also for the author: the entry's words 'if confirmed' about a 2025 approval can be settled; reports I opened say the United States regulator gave elamipretide (Forzinity, Stealth BioTherapeutics) an accelerated approval for Barth syndrome in September 2025.

findings.what: Registry entry NCT07921420 first posted: 'MF-300 for Treatment of Age-Related Sarcopenia', Epirium Bio; not yet recruiting; 225 people aged 65 and over; treatment for 24 weeks against placebo after an open first part; main measure a timed chair-stand test; estimated start 2027-01-01, main measurement 2028-06-01. The drug acts on an enzyme (15-PGDH), not on mitochondria.
Registry entry NCT07925853 first posted: Amazentis, 'Bioavailability of Two Mitopure Formulations', 24 healthy adults, a study of blood levels, not of muscle.

Registry entry NCT06274749 updated: National Institute on Aging, urolithin A against placebo in 180 people aged 55 and over; recruiting, estimated start 2026-11-12, main measurement 2027-03-31. Main measure is insulin release after a sugar drink, so a result would not meet this entry's test on muscle.

Registry entry NCT07531251 updated: Stealth BioTherapeutics' placebo-controlled trial of elamipretide in 48 people with Barth syndrome, recruiting. This is the confirming trial that goes with the 2025 accelerated approval for the rare disease, not a trial in age-related muscle loss.

HealthDay report that the United States regulator granted accelerated approval to Forzinity, the first treatment for Barth syndrome, on evidence of improved leg muscle strength. The page I opened gives the article date, 2025-09-25, not the approval date; a search summary (not opened) gives the approval date as 2025-09-19. The entry's notes say 'if confirmed'.
Food & Function: an analysis within a walnut-diet trial linking urolithins made in the gut to brain scans in older adults. Title only read; not a drug trial and not on muscle.

records.found: A preprint posted on 2026-11-06 gives a second published uptake figure: in state Medicaid programmes, prescriptions for the GLP-1 brands sold for weight rose from 20,449 in 2021 to 3,745,987 in 2025, with most of the rise coming after the heart and sleep apnoea approvals, and 41 states reporting Wegovy use by late 2024 though only 12 or 13 formally covered it for obesity. That points towards the earlier years of the wide-use estimate, because it shows the heart approval opening coverage that the weight-loss label could not; it is weakened by being one country and one payer, not yet peer-reviewed, not counted by purpose, and by an 80 per cent fall in the four states that ended coverage in early 2026. No new approval or trial report on the test came in the week; a meeting abstract and a pooled analysis, both dated 2026-11-02, agree with the existing stage.

findings.what: Staiger, preprint on Research Square: 'Utilization of and gross spending on anti-obesity GLP-1 receptor agonists in state Medicaid programs, 2021 to 2026'. From the federal State Drug Utilization Data: prescriptions 20,449 (2021) to 3,745,987 (2025); gross payments 24.7 million to 4.44 billion dollars; 41 states reported Wegovy use in the last quarter of 2024; California was 47 per cent of 2025 spending; prescriptions fell 80 per cent in early 2026 in four states that ended coverage. A preprint, not peer-reviewed; it counts brands, not the purpose of each prescription.

American Heart Association news release on abstract MDP1524 for its Scientific Sessions (Chicago, 2026-11-06 to 2026-11-09): in records of 256,492 adults with prediabetes and obesity and no diabetes, GLP-1 drug users had 15 per cent fewer heart attacks, 20 per cent fewer strokes and a 41 per cent lower risk of death than metformin users over about three years. Observational; the release says abstracts are not peer-reviewed. It does not meet the test, which asks for a controlled trial.

Marino and colleagues, Critical Pathways in Cardiology: pooled analysis of seven placebo-controlled semaglutide trials (38,412 people) finding 17 per cent fewer heart deaths, the same in people with overweight or obesity and no diabetes as in the other groups. Peer-reviewed; a pooling of trials already published, not a new trial.

Registry entry NCT07241390 updated: Eli Lilly's heart-outcomes trial of the GLP-1 tablet orforglipron against placebo, 7,140 people with heart or kidney disease, recruiting, main measurement due 2031-08. A second drug on the same road; no result.

Registry entry NCT07923630 (VITAL-H) first posted: semaglutide tablets are one of two drugs to be tested against placebo for the functional decline of ageing in 1,200 healthy people aged 60 to 75 without diabetes. It bears on the entry's question of whether these drugs act on ageing itself, not on the heart test.

Ohe, preprint on Research Square: pooled analysis of 162 placebo-controlled trials of GLP-1 drugs and tirzepatide finding serious falls and fractures not increased, with more loss of lean mass than placebo. Abstract read. A preprint.

records.found: The week itself brought only a trial design paper (metformin against placebo for three years in 212 people with a lung disease, published online 2026-11-04) and no sign of the TAME trial in the registry. But the entry lacks an older controlled trial that bears directly on its test: the MeMeMe trial (Diabetes Care, February 2025 issue) gave metformin or placebo to 1,442 people with metabolic syndrome for about three years and found roughly half as many new major diseases on metformin, a difference its authors say was fully explained by fewer cases of type 2 diabetes. The author should also know that a web page dated 2026-03-02 states that TAME has reported results; it cites no journal, registry number or other source, and nothing I opened supports it.

findings.what: Pasanisi and colleagues, Diabetes Care (February 2025 issue), the MeMeMe randomised trial: 1,442 people with metabolic syndrome given metformin or placebo, with or without a diet programme, followed three years on average. Main measure: new cases of major diseases (type 2 diabetes, heart and circulation disease, cancer). 6.7 and 6.9 cases per 100 person-years in the two metformin groups against 13.3 and 11.3 in the two placebo groups; 'the differences were fully explained by the reduction of type 2 diabetes'. Abstract read at Europe PMC. Not in the records. Whether it counts depends on whether the test's 'first age-related disease' includes diabetes; the test names heart disease, cancer and dementia.

de-Torres and colleagues, COPD journal (online 2026-11-04): design of AMICO, a placebo-controlled trial of metformin for 36 months in 212 people with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, described by its authors as the first trial of metformin as a treatment aimed at ageing in that disease. Main measure is lung function; new age-related illnesses are among the further measures. A design paper; the people have a disease, so it would not settle this test.

Registry entry NCT04264897 updated: the ANTHEM study (Oklahoma Medical Research Foundation), metformin against placebo for 12 weeks in 166 adults free of chronic disease. Completed; results were first posted on 2026-07-02 and show no significant difference on either main measure (insulin sensitivity; a measure of mitochondrial function in muscle). A short trial of markers, not of disease. Not in the records.

American Heart Association release on a meeting abstract: in records of 256,492 adults with prediabetes and obesity, metformin was the comparison drug and its users had more heart attacks, strokes and deaths than GLP-1 drug users. Observational, not peer-reviewed, and no untreated group, so it says little about metformin itself.
Registry search for the TAME trial by its full title on 2026-11-09 returns no entry (one unrelated study matched the words). Same as the record's check of 2026-10-17.

A page on the site iMedic headed as news that the TAME trial reported an 18 per cent reduction in age-related disease. It names the trial's lead investigator but cites no journal, DOI or registry number for any result, and links only to its own pages. It contradicts the record and every primary source; I treat it as unsupported.

The new federal trial against the decline of ageing (VITAL-H, NCT07923630) tests dapagliflozin and semaglutide, not metformin, and excludes people taking sugar-lowering drugs. A search summary (not opened) describes this as the government passing over TAME; that reading is the commentator's, not the registry's.

records.found: No controlled result on rapamycin in older people was published in the week. Two things the author should see: the registry entry posted on 2026-11-06 for the federal trial VITAL-H lists no rapamycin group, although the university's announcement of 2026-03-04 named rapamycin as one of its three drugs; and the entry lacks a controlled trial published on 2026-04-01 (RAPA-EX-01, 40 people aged 65 to 85) in which weekly rapamycin did not improve the gain from an exercise programme and, in two planned further analyses, did worse than placebo. A study of transplant records in GeroScience on 2026-11-05 found no survival difference with rapamycin; it belongs with the lifespan entry.

findings.what: Registry entry NCT07923630 (VITAL-H, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio) first posted with three groups: semaglutide tablets, dapagliflozin, placebo; 1,200 people. No rapamycin group.

The university's announcement of VITAL-H: 726 adults in their 60s, 'rapamycin, dapagliflozin and semaglutide' against placebo in four groups. A web search on 2026-11-09 found no statement that the rapamycin group was dropped or moved to another study, so the difference is unexplained, not confirmed as a withdrawal.

Stanfield and colleagues, Journal of Cachexia, Sarcopenia and Muscle, RAPA-EX-01: randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, 40 inactive adults aged 65 to 85, 13 weeks of weekly rapamycin or placebo alongside home exercise. Main measure (chair stands in 30 seconds): difference of -2.13 against rapamycin, not significant (p = 0.089); two planned sensitivity analyses favoured placebo significantly; more adverse events on rapamycin (99 against 63). Abstract read at Europe PMC. Not in the records.

Stewart and Fitzsimmons, GeroScience: among 11,474 kidney transplant recipients followed a median of 11 years, those prescribed rapamycin died at a similar age to those not (64.6 against 64.3 years). A records study at transplant doses, so outside this entry's test; it bears on the lifespan entry.

Journal of Cerebral Blood Flow & Metabolism (published 2026-09-10; news coverage on ScienceDaily dated 2026-11-05): a single-group pilot at the University of Missouri, four weeks of rapamycin in 23 adults aged 45 to 65, found increased blood flow in the brain in the 9 who carry the APOE4 gene variant and no change in the 14 who do not. No placebo group and middle-aged people, so it does not meet the test. Not in the records.
Registry entry NCT07166354 updated: a planned study of an mTOR-pathway drug for grey hair, not yet recruiting. Title and status only read from the dated list.
Biodexa company update (search summary, not opened): its rapamycin tablet is in a late-stage trial for an inherited bowel condition, 112 of 168 people enrolled. Not an ageing use.
